Title: September 10, 2026 - City of Boulder City Council Study Session (2027 Recommended Budget)
Overview: Council held a study session on the city manager's 2027 recommended budget, totaling $552.6 million across all funds with a $412-417 million operating budget and $135.4 million capital budget, reflecting a second-slowest growth rate since the pandemic and continued reductions. Staff walked through revenue assumptions, goal-area changes, the six-year CIP including wildfire, fire station, and facilities projects, and the long-term financial strategy, then answered council questions on Alpine Balsam oversight, reserves, the auditor function, snow and ice removal, photo enforcement, and possible wildfire funding increases. No formal budget changes were adopted; council members were directed to submit any substantive amendments with identified offsets to the hotline by September 28 ahead of the October 1 first reading.

Topic1.Title: Budget Overview and Revenue Assumptions
Topic1.Summary: Staff presented the 2027 recommended budget as balanced, with a $6.3 million general fund gap closed through ongoing reductions, realignments, and limited enhancements. Revenues are growing slowly, with sales and use tax up 3.3% and property tax up 6% after state legislation lowered assessed values. New revenue includes a transportation maintenance fee estimated at $3 million and a recreational marijuana tax increase from 3.5% to 5.5%. Utility rates rise 5% for water, 7% for wastewater, and 7% for stormwater.

Topic2.Title: Fund Our Future Community Engagement
Topic2.Summary: Staff summarized feedback from over 500 community members collected through in-person and online conversations on service trade-offs across 25 services in 12 categories. Top community priorities were wildfire resilience, municipal infrastructure and facilities maintenance, public safety, and affordable housing. Staff said this input was a key pillar for budget decisions.

Topic3.Title: Goal-Area Operating Budget Changes
Topic3.Summary: Scott Carpenter outlined changes by sustainability, equity, and resilience goal area. Notable items include $4.3 million for facilities maintenance, $11 million in total wildfire spending with a $300,000 climate-fund boost, three new police lieutenant positions, and $5.3 million for the Alpine Balsam affordable housing project. Reductions include Spruce Pool operations, East Boulder child watch services, and a $38,000 cut to microloan and rebate programs. The budget also funds the downtown ambassador program at $500,000 and a new community survey at $150,000.

Topic4.Title: Six-Year Capital Improvement Program
Topic4.Summary: Charlotte Husky presented the 2027 to 2032 CIP totaling $827.7 million, with about 75% directed to utilities and transportation. Key projects include a $13.5 million Barker gravity pipeline repair, Colorado 119 bus priority signal improvements, and $31.7 million to replace Fire Stations 2 and 4. Wildfire mitigation projects on open space total about $1.7 million for the OSP climate and wildfire plan, along with fuels and grazing projects. Facilities maintenance includes $27.9 million in new projects funded by the CCRS tax.

Topic5.Title: Long-Term Financial Strategy and Next Steps
Topic5.Summary: Staff described the long-term financial strategy, a comprehensive plan due in December, and ongoing structural issues tied to sales tax dependence and restricted revenues. Council was reminded that first reading is October 1 and adoption is October 15, with budget amendments due to the hotline by September 28 and required to include an identified offset. The recreational marijuana tax and several fee increases are part of the alternative funding mechanisms.

Topic6.Title: Alpine Balsam Project Oversight and Reporting
Topic6.Summary: Council members Kaplan and Robin asked how cost overruns and project updates are communicated to council and the public. Staff said the project remains within council-approved budgets across its 11-year history and that a story map and project page were published. Staff acknowledged the need for more detail on major projects and said financial systems could better tag cross-departmental work.

Topic7.Title: Reserves and Facility Replacement Funding
Topic7.Summary: Council asked whether reserves are set aside for facility replacement. Staff explained that a 2% current replacement value set-aside for buildings has been in place since facility strategic plan approval and is growing in the budget. Facilities staff clarified it funds ongoing replacement of building components, not wholesale rebuilding. Council members also asked about the 2026 bond and what happens to priority buildings if it fails.

Topic8.Title: Staffing and Fixed-Term Positions
Topic8.Summary: Council asked how fixed-term and one-time-funded positions will be sustained in future years. Staff said some have multi-year funding while others are reviewed annually against criticality. Council also raised the property tax outlook, and staff said no further legislative assessment cuts are expected, with about a 5% increase assumed per reassessment cycle.

Topic9.Title: Tiered Services Framework and Priority Alignment
Topic9.Summary: Nuria Rivera-Vandermark explained a new service tier framework: critically vital, federal and state mandated, city-mandated, strategic priority, and community enrichment. Council members asked why community-identified top priorities such as wildfire, snow and ice, public safety, and homelessness were not budgeted more clearly. Staff pointed to specific amounts for wildfire, facilities, police lieutenants, and affordable housing, and a council member said the spread was hard to track.

Topic10.Title: Spruce Pool, Silver Sneakers, and Pool Funding
Topic10.Summary: Council members questioned the Spruce Pool reduction and whether revenue from Silver Sneakers or sugar-sweetened beverage tax funds could keep it open. Staff explained that the sugar-sweetened beverage tax has voter-approved uses tied to health equity, and that many facility costs are outpacing revenue. Parks and recreation said senior discount structures will be reviewed in its 2027 work plan.

Topic11.Title: Auditor Function and Process
Topic11.Summary: Council discussed requests for an external performance auditor. Staff said the city has an internal auditor who can conduct performance audits and an external financial auditor selected by council. The internal audit committee screens community requests, and a public audit idea submission page was recently launched. Council agreed to schedule a future discussion on auditing in general.

Topic12.Title: Snow and Ice Removal Program
Topic12.Summary: Council member Winer asked whether west-side streets with senior residents will be added to snow and ice removal. Transportation staff said the extra funding supports weather diagnostic units but does not add streets this season, since last winter was mild and the program needs another season to evaluate. A packet on program changes will come to council within the next month.

Topic13.Title: Photo Enforcement Van Elimination
Topic13.Summary: Council asked why photo enforcement vans are being eliminated. Staff said costs outpaced revenue and that traffic patrol resources can respond instead. The police chief said neighborhoods with complaints will be prioritized, with motorcycle or car patrols, and the change will be monitored for any uptick in problems.

Topic14.Title: Wildfire Funding Recommendations and Grants
Topic14.Summary: Council member Benjamin proposed roughly $2 million in added climate initiative funding, $4 to 5 million in open space fuels management, and $2 to 3 million from new grants to expand wildfire mitigation. Other council members said the proposal was too large a climate cut and that it needed further staff review and a hotline submission. Staff noted wildfire grants total $2.2 million across five awards and that competitive grants are pursued selectively.

Topic15.Title: Policy Alignment and Community Connectors
Topic15.Summary: Council member Tina argued that budget reallocations at the end of the process bypass policy work, and that changes should come through adopted policy. Council member Adams raised concerns about nuisance enforcement on the Hill, San Lazaro annexation support, and cuts to the community connectors outreach component. Staff said these items would be reviewed or handled through separate appropriations, and that the funding question for outreach would be answered later.

Topic16.Title: Energy Costs, Evacuation Planning, and Water Supply
Topic16.Summary: Council member Adams questioned whether the budget accounts for rising energy and fuel costs, evacuation and recovery costs after wildfire, and water supply scenarios. Staff said capital project managers include energy costs in their projections and that the formula would be provided. Adams said these concerns would be submitted through the hotline.
